statement: In US adults with DSM-5 alcohol use disorder in a national household survey in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III; 60.1% response; Grant et al., 2015; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, which also ran the survey, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse; no conflicts declared), 7.7 in 100 of those who had the disorder in the past year and 19.8 in 100 of those who had had it at some time said they had sought treatment or help for it, counting 12-step groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous (the abstract calls this being treated). Seeking help rose with severity: 4.4, 8.7 and 34.7 in 100 of people with mild, moderate and severe lifetime disorder. Among people with the disorder in the past year, 4.5 in 100 had used 12-step groups, 3.6 in 100 a health care practitioner, 2.0 in 100 an outpatient service and 1.8 in 100 a rehabilitation programme. For other countries, a narrative review relays, second-hand, that 22.3 in 100 patients identified with alcohol dependence in primary care in six European countries received interventions, and 21.9 in 100 worldwide in an overview published in 2004 (Carvalho et al., 2019; two authors declare fees or grants from companies, including drug companies, outside the work). Help-seeking was self-reported at one interview, the survey did not cover most people who were in treatment, which would lower its figures, and 4 in 10 sampled people did not take part. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a US survey in 2012–2013, about 20 in 100 people who had ever had alcohol use disorder said they had ever looked for treatment or help, and about 8 in 100 of those who had it in the past year. Groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous were the most common kind of help. People with severe disorder looked for help more often (about 35 in 100) than people with mild disorder (about 4 in 100). A review passes on similar figures for Europe and the world, about 22 in 100. People reported this themselves, and the survey did not include most people who were in treatment at the time.
population: US adults with past-year or lifetime DSM-5 alcohol use disorder in NESARC-III (2012–2013); patients identified with alcohol dependence in primary care in six European countries and in a global overview (relayed second-hand)
exposure: Not applicable (a description of help-seeking); severity of the disorder (mild, moderate, severe)
outcome: Self-reported seeking of treatment or help for alcohol use disorder at any time, including 12-step groups, and its sources; receipt of interventions (European and global figures, second-hand)
magnitude: Grant et al. 2015 (NESARC-III): sought treatment or help, 7.7% (12-month DSM-5 AUD) and 19.8% (lifetime); DSM-IV 8.1% and 15.6% (2001–2002 NESARC: 7.2% and 14.0%); by severity, 12-month 2.7%, 4.9%, 21.3% and lifetime 4.4%, 8.7%, 34.7% (mild, moderate, severe); sources among 12-month AUD: 12-step groups 4.5%, health care practitioners 3.6%, outpatient facilities 2.0%, rehabilitation programmes 1.8%; lifetime AUD: rehabilitation 9.0%, practitioners 8.7%; mean age at first treatment 29.4 years. Carvalho et al. 2019 (second-hand): 22.3% of patients identified with alcohol dependence in primary care in six European countries received interventions (more than 13 000 patients, 358 general practitioners); 21.9% in a global overview (2004).

evidence.locator: Results › Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Among respondents with 12-month and lifetime DSM-5 AUD, 7.7% and 19.8% had sought treatment or help for AUD (DSM-IV AUD: 8.1% and 15.6%, against 7.2% and 14.0% in the 2001–2002 NESARC). Among those with 12-month AUD, 4.5% had received help from 12-step groups, 3.6% from health care practitioners, 2.0% from outpatient facilities and 1.8% from rehabilitation programmes; for lifetime AUD, rehabilitation programmes 9.0% and practitioners 8.7%. By severity, 2.7%, 4.9% and 21.3% (mild, moderate and severe 12-month AUD) and 4.4%, 8.7% and 34.7% (lifetime AUD) had sought help. Mean age at first treatment 29.4 years. The abstract words the lifetime figure as ever treated.

evidence.locator: Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: NESARC-III interviewed 36,309 US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 or older face to face, April 2012 to June 2013, in households and selected group quarters; screener response 72.0%, person response 84.0%, total 60.1%; data weighted for oversampling and non-response and post-stratified to the 2012 American Community Survey. The authors state that homeless people, prisoners and most people in treatment are not covered, which may lead to underestimation.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 173 (claim writer), from AI reader 159's study card

evidence.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The Seminar relays that in a study of more than 13 000 patients and 358 general practitioners in six European countries, 22.3% of patients identified with alcohol dependence received interventions, and that the most recent global overview gave almost the same figure, 21.9%, with lower treatment rates in some countries such as the USA. Editors' note: by the reference list, the European figure is from Rehm et al. (2015) and the global one from Kohn et al. (2004); neither source was read.

risk_of_bias.note: Study card sc_grant_2015 (JBI prevalence checklist), overall moderate: help-seeking was self-reported at one interview and over a lifetime; 60.1% response; the frame leaves out most people in treatment, which biases help-seeking down.

inconsistency.note: The second-hand European and global figures (about 22 in 100) are close to the US lifetime figure (about 20 in 100), though they measure receipt of interventions rather than help-seeking.

indirectness.note: Worded for US adults in 2012–2013 and the survey's measure (seeking treatment or help, including 12-step groups).

imprecision.note: Large sample; the severity subgroups are reported as the paper prints them.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a national survey.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim: starts low and is never upgraded. Rated down one level for risk of bias (self-report, response, and a frame that misses most people in treatment), giving very low. The measure is seeking treatment or help, including 12-step groups; the abstract calls it being treated, a wording the claim does not adopt. The European and global figures are relayed second-hand by a narrative review and are not graded. Status single study: one survey read; the second-hand figures agree in size but were not read.
